source_text: erator ipse atque Salvator his qui ei dixerant, ut exiret de Ierosolymis: Ecce, inquit, eicio daemonia, et sanitates perficio hodie et cras, et tertia consummor Quomodo manent peccata reatu, quae praeterierunt actu; sic e contrario fieri potest, ut concupiscentia maneat actu, et praetereat reatu
pass_a_gloss: Erator himself and Salvator these who to-him dixerant, so-that/as exiret about/from Ierosolymis: behold, he-says, eicio of-a-demon, and sanitates to-be-perfected today and tomorrow, and tertia consummor how manent sins in-guilt, which praeterierunt actu; thus from contrario to-become is-able, so-that/as desire maneat actu, and praetereat in-guilt.

lemmas.lexica: LS peccatum=fault, error; Blaise Christian sin
LS concupiscentia=eager desire; Blaise Christian usage often sexual desire vs nuptiae

pass_b_english: I cannot imagine in what dialectical treatise you found that all opposites can be reversed.
In no dialectical treatise can it be found that all opposites can be reversed.

choices.why: Julian's forensic/moral fault tied to will, not a substance in nature.
Julian distinguishes nuptiae from concupiscentia; do not flatten to 'lust' as a nature-sin substance.

anf_compare.notes: Victorian English of some of Julian survives inside NPNF Augustine (chiefly On Marriage and Concupiscence and related anti-Pelagian books). NPNF was not copied. Pass A is a literal gloss of Augustinus.it Latin of Julian's words only; Augustine's replies in the same locus are excluded. Julian is not first-English.

speaker: Julian of Eclanum (words preserved in Augustine, Contra Iulianum / Against Julian), including authorities Julian quoted; Augustine's reply at this locus is excluded.
